blocks.text: Pipeline parallelism splits a model into sequential stages assigned to different devices, similar to the simple layer level model parallelism covered earlier in this module, but adds the specific technique of micro-batching to keep every device more consistently busy rather than sitting idle waiting for earlier stages.

This topic addresses the device idle time problem raised at the end of the Model Parallelism topic directly, explaining how pipeline parallelism turns a naive layer split into a genuinely efficient distributed training approach.

Pipeline parallelism organizes a model computation into a sequence of stages, each assigned to a different device, data flows through these stages in order, similar to an assembly line, with each device handling its specific portion of the overall computation.
2. Splitting the Model Into Sequential Stages

blocks.alt: Splitting the Model Into Sequential Stages

blocks.text: This is structurally similar to the layer level model parallelism introduced in the earlier Model Parallelism topic, one device holds a set of early layers, another holds the middle layers, and so on, but pipeline parallelism specifically addresses the device utilization problem that basic approach runs into.

Without any special handling, processing one batch through a sequential pipeline means each stage device sits idle until the previous stage finishes and passes along its output, a wasted idle period called a pipeline bubble, exactly the underutilization risk raised at the end of the earlier Model Parallelism topic.

Pipeline parallelism addresses this idle time by splitting a batch into several smaller micro-batches and feeding them through the pipeline in a staggered, overlapping fashion, so while stage one processes the second micro-batch, stage two is already working on the first, keeping devices busier overall and shrinking those wasted bubble periods.

code.content:
# A conceptual sketch of pipeline parallelism with micro-batches
micro_batches = split_into_micro_batches(full_batch, num_chunks=4)
for i, micro_batch in enumerate(micro_batches):
    stage1_output = stage1_device(micro_batch)
    # Stage 2 can start working on an earlier micro-batch's output
    # while stage 1 continues with the next one, overlapping work

blocks.text: Compared to tensor parallelism, covered in the previous topic, which requires communication multiple times within every single layer, pipeline parallelism only needs communication at the boundaries between stages, a coarser, less frequent communication pattern that tolerates a slower device interconnect better.

blocks.text: Because data only needs to transfer between devices at each stage boundary, rather than throughout the internal computation of each layer, pipeline parallelism communication overhead is generally lower than tensor parallelism, making it a more forgiving choice when devices are not connected through an especially fast link.

blocks.title: This connects the last two topics together clearly
blocks.content: Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism represent two different points on a communication frequency versus splitting granularity spectrum, and real large scale training setups sometimes combine both alongside data parallelism.

blocks.text: For pipeline parallelism to work well, the stages need to be reasonably balanced in computational cost, an uneven split, where one stage does far more work than another, leaves the lighter stage devices waiting on the heavier one, undermining the micro-batching efficiency gains covered earlier in this topic.
8. Combining Pipeline Parallelism With Other Techniques

Pipeline parallelism is often combined with data parallelism, covered earlier in this module, replicating an entire pipeline of stages to process multiple batches simultaneously, and sometimes with tensor parallelism as well for models large enough to need both finer grained and coarser grained splitting at once.

Pipeline parallelism makes the most sense for very deep models that need to be split across several devices where the interconnect between those devices is not fast enough to comfortably support tensor parallelism, offering a reasonable middle ground between simple, inefficient layer splitting and the higher communication demands of tensor parallelism.

A team splitting a very deep model across four devices using a naive layer split notices significant idle time, with later stage devices frequently waiting on earlier ones to finish before they have anything to work on.

Introducing micro-batching, splitting each training batch into several smaller pieces fed through the pipeline in a staggered, overlapping way, meaningfully reduces this idle time, keeping all four devices busier throughout training and improving overall training throughput without needing the faster interconnect tensor parallelism would require.

Choosing pipeline parallelism when the model would have fit on a single device with simpler data parallelism
Confusing pipeline parallelism's stage boundaries with tensor parallelism's within-layer splitting

Pipeline parallelism splits a model into sequential stages across devices and uses micro-batching to keep those devices busier throughout training, addressing the idle time problem a naive layer split runs into, and its comparatively infrequent, stage boundary communication pattern makes it more forgiving of slower device interconnects than tensor parallelism.
